<reason>CON won a close debate by making the live clash easier to decide: once both sides impose a floor, a public statute that binds strangers is the honest tool, while state-extended sectoral deals are incumbent contracts scored as coverage. PRO had a strong scale-and-calibration case and a real turn that CON’s rigidity worries also hit a blunt national minimum, but CON answered the outsourced-cleaner pressure with a coherent alternative and kept converting PRO’s “all floors impose” move into a reason to reject the motion rather than adopt it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON’s pressure on the holdout contractor, then the R2/closing conversion of PRO’s imposition concession: law may bind strangers; a bargain made binding on firms that would reject it is industrial regulation, and a coverage statistic can hide priced-out first jobs.</best_rebuttal>
